# 2026-07-26 · Rotating refresh tokens for login flow

Change ID: `rotating-refresh-tokens`
Created: `2026-07-26T20:54:26+09:00`
Risk: R3
Status: In progress

## Problem and intended outcome

`src/auth/session.py` issued a single long-lived (90-day) refresh token per
login that stayed valid until someone noticed a leak and revoked it by hand.
Nothing in the module could distinguish a leaked token from the legitimate
one, so a copied token was as good as the real one for up to 90 days.

The intended outcome: every redemption of a refresh token consumes it and
returns a new one in the same token family (rotation), and redeeming a token
that was already rotated away — which can only happen if a second party got
a copy of it — revokes the rest of that family automatically (reuse
detection), forcing re-login instead of relying on manual revocation.

## Success and non-goals

Success is that a stolen refresh token is unusable after the legitimate
client's next refresh (or, if the attacker refreshes first, that the
legitimate client's subsequent use is detected and the family is killed),
without changing access-token issuance or the 15-minute access token
lifetime.

Not in scope: persistence layer (the store stays in-memory, matching the
existing module — see "Known limits" below), transport/HTTP layer for the
login and refresh endpoints (no such endpoint exists yet in this repo),
device/IP binding, and alerting on reuse events.

## Existing responsibilities searched

`src/auth/session.py` already owned refresh token issuance, expiry, and
revocation, so rotation and reuse detection were added there rather than in
a new module. The prior API (`issue_refresh_token`, `is_refresh_valid`,
`revoke`) had no consumers outside this module and its tests (confirmed via
repo-wide search), so it was replaced rather than kept alongside a new API.

## System and data flow

Login -> `start_session()` mints the first token of a new family.
Refresh -> `rotate(old_token)`:
  - unknown / expired / already-revoked-family -> `KeyError`
  - already rotated away (reuse) -> revoke family, raise `RefreshTokenReused`
  - otherwise -> mark old token rotated, mint and return a new token in the
    same family
Logout / incident response -> `revoke_family(family_id)` invalidates every
token descended from that login.

## Decisions and trade-offs

See ADR `docs/engineering/decisions/rotating-refresh-tokens.md` for the
reuse-detection design (family revocation vs. single-token revocation).

Kept the existing in-memory `dict`/`set` storage model rather than
introducing persistence in this change, to keep the rotation logic isolated
and reviewable. This is a real limitation for a production deployment — see
"Known limits" below.

## Failure, security, and recovery

See the threat model at `docs/engineering/security/rotating-refresh-tokens.md`
for attacker-controlled inputs, invariants, and abuse cases in detail.

Failure mode if rotation has a bug that fails open: a rotated-away token
would stay valid, silently reverting to the old non-rotating behavior.
Mitigated by the test suite asserting the old token is invalid immediately
after rotation (`test_rotating_invalidates_the_old_token`) and that reuse is
detected even several rotations later
(`test_reuse_after_the_fact_still_revokes_the_family`).

Recovery: `revoke_family(family_id)` is the operational lever for both
self-service logout and incident response (force logout on suspected
compromise). See the runbook for on-call steps.

Rollback: revert this commit. No data migration is involved since storage
stayed in-memory; there is no persisted state to roll back.

## Verification evidence

`python3 -m unittest discover -s tests` — 12 tests passed on 2026-07-26
(3 pre-existing + 9 new: rotation issues a new token, rotation invalidates
the old token, expired tokens can't rotate, unknown tokens raise, reuse is
detected, reuse revokes the rest of the family, reuse is still detected
after several further rotations, family revocation invalidates the current
token, family revocation blocks further rotation, and two sessions' families
stay independent).

No integration or load-bearing runtime seam exists yet because there is no
login/refresh HTTP endpoint in this repository — `src/auth/session.py` is a
standalone module. This is recorded as a known limit, not silently assumed
to be covered.

## Known limits and learning gaps

- Storage is in-memory (module-level `dict`/`set`), matching what was already
  there. A process restart drops all sessions and family revocations. Before
  this lands behind a real login endpoint, the store needs to move to a
  shared/persistent backend (e.g. Redis or the primary DB) so rotation state
  survives restarts and is shared across instances.
- No login/refresh HTTP endpoint exists in this repo to wire this module into,
  so there is no end-to-end (request-level) verification, only unit-level
  verification of the state machine itself.
- No alerting/metric is emitted when `RefreshTokenReused` fires. An operator
  currently has no way to see a reuse event happen; the runbook documents how
  to check for one by hand until that's added.
- Family ids and tokens are unbounded in the in-memory store (no expiry
  sweep). Long-running processes will accumulate rotated/expired token
  records. Not a correctness issue for this change, but worth a follow-up
  before production load.

## References

- ADR: `docs/engineering/decisions/rotating-refresh-tokens.md`
- Threat model: `docs/engineering/security/rotating-refresh-tokens.md`
- Runbook: `docs/engineering/runbooks/rotating-refresh-tokens.md`

# 2026-07-26 · Rotating refresh tokens for login flow

Change ID: `rotating-refresh-tokens`
Created: `2026-07-26T20:54:26+09:00`
Status: Accepted

## Context

The prior design issued one refresh token per login that stayed valid for 90
days regardless of use. A leaked token (via XSS, log exposure, a compromised
device, etc.) was indistinguishable from the legitimate one and remained
usable until someone noticed and revoked it by hand. We need a design that
detects theft automatically instead of depending on manual revocation.

## Options considered

1. **Rotation only, no reuse detection.** Redeeming a token consumes it and
   issues a new one; an old token is simply invalid afterward. Cheapest to
   build, but a race between the attacker and the legitimate client just
   picks whichever redeems first — the loser is silently locked out with no
   signal that theft happened.
2. **Rotation + reuse detection, revoke only the reused token.** Same as
   below but only the specific reused token is invalidated, leaving the rest
   of the chain (and thus the session) alive.
3. **Rotation + reuse detection, revoke the whole token family.** Every
   token descended from one login shares a family id. Redeeming an
   already-rotated token proves two parties held a token that was supposed
   to be single-use; since we can't tell which party is the attacker, we
   revoke every token in the family and force re-login.

## Decision

Choose option 3. Once a rotated-away token is redeemed, the chain of custody
is broken — both the legitimate client and the attacker may hold a live
token derived from the same lineage, and there's no signal in this module to
tell them apart. Revoking only the single reused token (option 2) would
leave an attacker-derived token from a later rotation still valid if they'd
already moved past the point of reuse. Full-family revocation is the only
option that closes that gap, at the cost of also logging out the legitimate
client — an acceptable trade given the alternative is leaving a
theft-in-progress session open.

## Consequences and reversal

A detected reuse always forces re-login for that session, even in the
(unprovable) case where the "reuse" was caused by a legitimate client retry
racing a rotation rather than actual theft. This is a deliberate
false-positive bias toward safety. Reversal is reverting the commit; there
is no persisted state to migrate since storage is in-memory (see the change
brief's "Known limits").

## Implementation references

- `src/auth/session.py` (`rotate`, `RefreshTokenReused`, `revoke_family`)

## Supersession

"""Login sessions.

Refresh tokens rotate on every use: redeeming a refresh token consumes it and
returns a new one in the same token family. The old token stops being valid
immediately, not just eventually, so a copy of it is only useful to whoever
redeems it first.

Every token traces back to one login through its family id. If a token that
was already rotated away is redeemed again, that means two parties ended up
holding what was meant to be a single-use token: the legitimate client (who
already moved on) and whoever else copied it. There is no way to tell which
is which after the fact, so reuse revokes the whole family rather than just
the reused token.
"""

import secrets
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

ACCESS_TOKEN_MINUTES = 15
REFRESH_TOKEN_DAYS = 90


class RefreshTokenReused(Exception):
    """A rotated-away refresh token was redeemed again.

    Its family has already been revoked by the time this is raised.
    """

    def __init__(self, family_id: str):
        super().__init__(f"refresh token reuse detected for family {family_id!r}")
        self.family_id = family_id


@dataclass
class _Token:
    family_id: str
    issued_at: datetime
    rotated: bool = False


_TOKENS: dict[str, _Token] = {}
_REVOKED_FAMILIES: set[str] = set()


def start_session(now: datetime | None = None) -> tuple[str, str]:
    """Issue the first refresh token for a new login.

    Returns (token, family_id). Keep the family id only if you need to revoke
    the session directly (e.g. on logout); redeeming tokens does not require it.
    """
    family_id = secrets.token_urlsafe(16)
    return _mint(family_id, now), family_id


def rotate(token: str, now: datetime | None = None) -> str:
    """Redeem a refresh token for a new one in the same family.

    Raises KeyError for a token that is unknown, expired, or already revoked.
    Raises RefreshTokenReused if the token was already rotated away; the rest
    of the family is revoked as a side effect before the exception is raised,
    so the caller should force re-login rather than retry.
    """
    moment = now or datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    record = _TOKENS.get(token)
    if record is None or record.family_id in _REVOKED_FAMILIES:
        raise KeyError("unknown or revoked refresh token")
    if moment >= refresh_expires_at(record.issued_at):
        raise KeyError("expired refresh token")
    if record.rotated:
        _REVOKED_FAMILIES.add(record.family_id)
        raise RefreshTokenReused(record.family_id)
    record.rotated = True
    return _mint(record.family_id, moment)


def is_refresh_valid(token: str, now: datetime | None = None) -> bool:
    moment = now or datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    record = _TOKENS.get(token)
    if record is None or record.rotated or record.family_id in _REVOKED_FAMILIES:
        return False
    return moment < refresh_expires_at(record.issued_at)


def refresh_expires_at(issued_at: datetime) -> datetime:
    return issued_at + timedelta(days=REFRESH_TOKEN_DAYS)


def revoke_family(family_id: str) -> None:
    """Revoke every token descended from one login, e.g. on logout."""
    _REVOKED_FAMILIES.add(family_id)


def _mint(family_id: str, now: datetime | None = None) -> str:
    token = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
    _TOKENS[token] = _Token(family_id=family_id, issued_at=now or datetime.now(timezone.utc))
    return token

import unittest
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

from src.auth.session import RefreshTokenReused, is_refresh_valid, revoke_family, rotate, start_session


class SessionCase(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_a_fresh_session_token_is_valid(self):
        token, _family_id = start_session()
        self.assertTrue(is_refresh_valid(token))

    def test_rotating_issues_a_new_token(self):
        token, _family_id = start_session()
        new_token = rotate(token)
        self.assertNotEqual(token, new_token)
        self.assertTrue(is_refresh_valid(new_token))

    def test_rotating_invalidates_the_old_token(self):
        token, _family_id = start_session()
        rotate(token)
        self.assertFalse(is_refresh_valid(token))

    def test_redeeming_an_expired_token_raises(self):
        issued = datetime.now(timezone.utc) - timedelta(days=91)
        token, _family_id = start_session(now=issued)
        with self.assertRaises(KeyError):
            rotate(token)

    def test_redeeming_an_unknown_token_raises(self):
        with self.assertRaises(KeyError):
            rotate("not-a-real-token")

    def test_reusing_a_rotated_token_is_detected(self):
        token, _family_id = start_session()
        rotate(token)
        with self.assertRaises(RefreshTokenReused):
            rotate(token)

    def test_reuse_revokes_the_rest_of_the_family(self):
        token, _family_id = start_session()
        latest = rotate(token)
        with self.assertRaises(RefreshTokenReused):
            rotate(token)
        self.assertFalse(is_refresh_valid(latest))

    def test_reuse_after_the_fact_still_revokes_the_family(self):
        token, _family_id = start_session()
        latest = rotate(token)
        latest = rotate(latest)
        with self.assertRaises(RefreshTokenReused):
            rotate(token)
        self.assertFalse(is_refresh_valid(latest))

    def test_revoking_a_family_invalidates_its_current_token(self):
        token, family_id = start_session()
        revoke_family(family_id)
        self.assertFalse(is_refresh_valid(token))

    def test_revoking_a_family_blocks_further_rotation(self):
        token, family_id = start_session()
        revoke_family(family_id)
        with self.assertRaises(KeyError):
            rotate(token)

    def test_two_sessions_have_independent_families(self):
        token_a, _family_a = start_session()
        token_b, family_b = start_session()
        revoke_family(family_b)
        self.assertTrue(is_refresh_valid(token_a))
        self.assertFalse(is_refresh_valid(token_b))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()
